title: Auth Control Plane signing JWKS (v1 wire format)
description:
The JWKS document (RFC 7517 JWK Set, narrowed) carrying the PUBLIC Ed25519 signing keys of one issuer: the document served at /.well-known/jwks.json (TRD sections 12 and 15) and read by resource-service verifiers. It lists the active key and, during a rotation, the overlap keys: a new key is published BEFORE anything is signed with it, and the retired public key stays until the last token it signed has expired plus skew (TRD section 12), so two or more keys is the normal rotation case rather than an edge case. A consumer that meets an unknown `kid` refreshes once, boundedly, and then denies: that behaviour cannot be expressed in a schema and is a consumer rule.

The real consumer is dev-health-go's `authverify.Ed25519JWKSVerifier.Keys()`, which the Go corpus runs over every fixture. The contract's job is to pin the handshake and to stop a schema from being LOOSER than that consumer (it would certify documents the reader refuses) or STRICTER in an undeclared way.

ONE ISSUER, ONE KEY USE. Platform access/workload-token keys and ACR Web-assertion keys are separate issuers (TRD section 12). A JWKS has no issuer member (`additionalProperties: false` below), so the binding is made by discovery: a verifier reaches this JWKS only through the `jwks_uri` of a discovery document (discovery.v1) from the issuer it has pinned for that credential class. See discovery.v1.schema.json.

PRIVATE MEMBERS ARE ABSENT FROM THE SCHEMA ENTIRELY. `d`, `p`, `q`, `dp`, `dq`, `qi` and `k` are not declared under `properties` and `additionalProperties` is false, so a JWKS carrying any of them fails. This is subtractive on purpose: the leak is unrepresentable rather than prohibited. Each member has its own reject fixture, and a test asserts none is declared.

EVERY CONSTRAINT BELOW WAS READ OFF THE CONSUMER, NOT CHOSEN. authverify.Keys() rejects the whole document unless every key satisfies kty=OKP, crv=Ed25519, alg=EdDSA, use empty or "sig", a kid that is non-empty after TrimSpace and at most 256 BYTES, and an x that base64.RawURLEncoding decodes to exactly 32 bytes; it decodes with DisallowUnknownFields, refuses an empty keys array, and refuses a repeated kid. A schema that permits more than that would certify documents the only consumer refuses.

THIS SCHEMA IS DELIBERATELY NARROWER THAN THE CONSUMER, AND THE LIST IS A CORPUS RATHER THAN A SENTENCE. Every narrowing has a fixture under examples/jwks/ in the manifest's narrower_than_consumer category, and a test asserts BOTH halves of each: the consumer accepts it, this schema refuses it.

The first version of this file listed the narrowings in prose here and got the list wrong -- it declared two and there were five. Codex round 1 blocked it. The list moved into fixtures because a sentence cannot be executed, and the test that was supposed to police this direction passed the whole time: none of the twenty reject fixtures happened to exercise any of the missing four.

The narrowings, each with a fixture AND a predicate. Round 2 blocked this contract because `use: ""` had a predicate and this sentence and no fixture -- the round-1 defect committed inside its own fix. A test now enforces the correspondence in both directions, because remembering to add both is what failed twice.

The narrowings:
  * CASE-VARIANT MEMBER NAMES. Go's encoding/json matches struct field names case-INSENSITIVELY, and DisallowUnknownFields compares after that match, so the consumer reads {"KEYS":[{"KTY":...}]} as an ordinary document and accepts it. Refused here because JSON Schema matches property names EXACTLY: admitting case variants would mean enumerating every casing of every member in `properties` and rewriting `required` as a disjunction over all of them, and would leave the wire form with no canonical spelling for a producer to target. An earlier version of this note said instead that admitting casings makes additionalProperties:false unenforceable -- executed and FALSE, a schema declaring both `keys` and `KEYS` still rejects an undeclared `issuer`. The narrowing is right; that reason was not.
  * `use: null`. Decodes to Go's zero string, so the consumer sees an empty use. Refused here; absence is how this contract says nothing.
  * A `kid` with surrounding whitespace. The consumer trims before testing for empty, so it accepts, and a token's kid header would then have to carry the UNTRIMMED value to resolve.
  * A `kid` containing NUL. unicode.IsSpace(NUL) is false, so TrimSpace does not strip it and the consumer accepts.
  * `use: ""`. Tolerated by the consumer alongside "sig"; refused here for the same reason as null -- a field present and blank says nothing its absence does not.

THE LIST IS NOW CLOSED BY PROPERTY, NOT BY ROUND. contracts/auth/v1/sweeps/jwks.property-sweep.json enumerates every member and value class on which this schema and the consumer can differ, with a literal verdict for each, and the Go, Python and ajv runners all execute it (the Go one against the real consumer). Each narrowing belongs to exactly one class named here, and a test fails if a class is missing from this description or has no row:
  * [N1] Member names. The consumer matches by Unicode simple folding, this schema exactly: KEYS, Keys, keyſ (U+017F), Kelvin-sign K, at the top level and in a key.
  * [N2] `use: null`: the consumer reads the empty use.
  * [N3] `use: ""`: tolerated by the consumer.
  * [N4] Any `kid` character outside U+0021..U+007E, anywhere in the value: control, format, space separators, combining marks, CJK, emoji and their sequences, U+FFFD, DEL. The consumer refuses only a kid that is empty after TrimSpace, so all of these are accepted, and surrounding whitespace is trimmed before the test. Every Unicode category outside printable ASCII has its own entry, and every printable ASCII character is accepted by both.
  * [N5] The 256-byte kid bound. The consumer applies it AFTER TrimSpace, so 256 bytes plus any amount of padding is accepted; this schema refuses the padding characters (they are outside U+0021..U+007E) and never sees a trimmed length.
  * [N6] `x` containing CR or LF. The consumer's base64 decoding skips them, so a 43-character key followed by a line feed decodes to 32 bytes and is accepted; the 43-character pattern refuses it. Every validator must refuse it: Python's `$` matches before a final newline, so the loader compiles patterns with strictly_anchored, and the sweep's trailing-newline rows fail if that is removed.
  * [C1] A repeated kid, which the schema cannot see (it declares no uniqueItems, so even two identical keys validate); the consumer refuses it.
  * [C2] A repeated member name inside one JSON object. Parsers keep the last value, so the schema sees one member; the consumer refuses the bytes. The sweep also lists, as raw bytes, the byte-layer inputs on which the consumer and a parsing validator part or agree: trailing content, a BOM, invalid UTF-8, unpaired surrogate escapes, comments and a trailing comma.
Where both sides refuse, or both accept, the row is an agreement and needs no class.

`kid` IS RESTRICTED TO PRINTABLE NON-SPACE ASCII, and the reason is a counting mismatch, not aesthetics. The consumer bounds kid at 256 BYTES; JSON Schema's maxLength counts CODE POINTS. A kid of 256 U+00E9 characters is 256 code points and 512 bytes: maxLength 256 accepts it and the consumer refuses it. A one-byte-per-character alphabet makes the two counts the same number. Excluding space ALSO refuses a whitespace-only kid, which minLength cannot -- but note this is NOT equivalent to the consumer's TrimSpace rule, and an earlier version of this file claimed it was: the class is strictly narrower, which is why two of the fixtures above exist.

`x` IS PINNED TO 43 CHARACTERS rather than described as "base64url". 43 characters of the base64url alphabet always decode to exactly 32 bytes, so one pattern closes three classes at once: padding (the consumer's RawURLEncoding rejects `=`, Python's urlsafe_b64decode accepts it), the standard `+/` alphabet (same split), and wrong key length. Verified by sampling 200000 random 43-character base64url strings: every one decoded to exactly 32 bytes, none errored.

ON THE WRONG-LENGTH CASE SPECIFICALLY, because the first version of this file overstated it: ed25519.Verify does PANIC on a 31- or 33-byte public key rather than returning an error, and both languages' base64 decoders do accept those lengths. But THE CONSUMER GUARDS THIS ITSELF -- Keys() compares the decoded length against ed25519.PublicKeySize before returning a key -- so the panic is not reachable through it. This pattern is defence-in-depth and a statement of the wire form, not the only thing standing between a malformed document and a crash. That claim was written after reading the very function that disproves it.

TWO CLASSES THIS SCHEMA CANNOT REACH, both enforced by the consumer or by nothing, both in the manifest:
  * A REPEATED kid. This schema declares no uniqueItems, and one would compare whole array items in any case, so two keys sharing a kid pass. The consumer refuses the document. Covered by the reject_by_client corpus and class [C1].
  * TRAILING CONTENT and DUPLICATE MEMBERS. Both are byte-layer rules the schema never sees. The consumer (dev-health-go v0.24.7, Keys()) refuses a second JSON value after the document and a repeated member name before decoding; the byte layer is executed as raw bytes by the sweep's byte-layer rows and by the raw-text generator in jwks_byte_layer_differential_test.go (CHAOS-4956).

keys.description: The signing keys, most commonly one. Two appear during a rotation, while tokens signed by the outgoing kid are still within their TTL. The consumer refuses an EMPTY array rather than treating it as "no keys yet": a JWKS that parses but yields nothing would make every verification fail with a lookup miss instead of a configuration error, which is the same symptom as an unknown kid and sends the reader to the wrong place.

items.description: One Ed25519 public signing key (RFC 8037 OKP). `additionalProperties: false` mirrors the consumer's json.Decoder.DisallowUnknownFields, which rejects the ENTIRE document on one unrecognised member. That is stricter than RFC 7517, which says an unrecognised JWK member must be ignored, and the strictness is inherited deliberately rather than softened: a schema that ignored unknown members would accept documents the only consumer refuses, which is the failure this contract exists to prevent. It also makes the subtractive guarantee automatic -- `d`, the private scalar, is refused because it is not listed, so a JWKS cannot carry the private half even by accident.

kty.description: RFC 8037 octet key pair. The consumer compares this literally; RSA and EC keys are refused before any key material is examined.

crv.description: The signing curve. X25519 is the same key TYPE (OKP) and is for key agreement, never signatures, so it is refused here rather than later at a confusing verification failure.

alg.description: REQUIRED, though RFC 7517 makes `alg` optional. The consumer compares it literally against "EdDSA", so an absent `alg` reads as "" and the document is refused. Pinning it also removes the algorithm-confusion question at the key level rather than only at the token header.

use.description: OPTIONAL. Present, it must say `sig`; the consumer refuses any other value. Its absence is the ordinary case and means the same thing.

kid.description: The key identifier a token's `kid` header is matched against. Printable non-space ASCII, 1..256 characters -- which is also 1..256 BYTES, and that equality is the point: see the schema-level note on why maxLength cannot express the consumer's byte bound. Operator-settable, so the alphabet is kept wide enough for any reasonable value rather than pinned to the default's shape.

x.description: The raw 32-byte Ed25519 public key, base64url, unpadded (RFC 7515 section 2). Exactly 43 characters of the URL-safe alphabet: see the schema-level note for why the character count rather than a `format` or a prose description is what makes this safe. Carries the PUBLIC half only -- the private scalar `d` is not a permitted member.
